title: What LLMs Actually Understand (and What They Don't)
summary: LLMs do more than autocomplete and less than a colleague. What research shows about how they handle language, where it breaks and how to match your checks to the stakes.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The printer by the meeting room takes a few seconds to wake up. While it warms, you paste a confusing product requirement into a chat window and ask what it means. The answer lands before the first page does. It's tidy, it uses your team's vocabulary, and it even guesses the question you were about to ask next. For a moment it feels like talking to a patient colleague.

That feeling is where most confusion about large language models starts. "It understands me" is a fine shortcut in casual talk. When you're deciding whether to ship, sign or trust something, you need a sharper version of the word. This post covers what researchers have found about how LLMs handle language, where that breaks down, and how to set your checks to match.

Why it feels like understanding

An LLM is trained to predict the next piece of text across an enormous amount of writing. To do that well, it has to pick up a lot of structure: grammar, facts that show up often, how arguments usually unfold, what kind of answer tends to follow what kind of question. That's why it can summarize a messy meeting note, explain a function or draft a test plan in seconds.

Whether that counts as understanding is a live argument, even among experts. In a 2022 survey of NLP researchers, respondents split almost exactly in half on whether language models understand language (NLP Community Metasurvey). On one side, Emily Bender and Alexander Koller argued that a system trained only on form, the surface of text, has no way in principle to learn meaning, which they define as the link between words and what a speaker intends to communicate (Bender and Koller, 2020). On the other, Melanie Mitchell and David Krakauer suggest we may be looking at a different mode of understanding with its own strengths and limits, and that the useful work is mapping them (Mitchell and Krakauer).

You don't have to settle that debate to use these tools well. You do need a rough picture of what goes on inside.

What researchers see inside the model

In March 2025, Anthropic's interpretability team published traces of what happens inside Claude 3.5 Haiku while it answers (Tracing the thoughts of a large language model). Some of it looks a lot like reasoning:

  • Asked for the capital of the state that contains Dallas, the model first represents "Dallas is in Texas," then "the capital of Texas is Austin." When the researchers swapped the Texas concept for California, the answer changed to Sacramento. The middle step really drives the answer.
  • When writing a rhyming couplet, it picks the rhyme word before it writes the line that leads there. It plans ahead.

Some of it should make you careful:

  • For 36 + 59, the model runs one path that estimates roughly and another that works out the last digit exactly. Ask it how it did the sum and it describes the carry-the-one method from school. Its account of its own process didn't match the process.
  • Given a hint about the expected answer to a hard math problem, it sometimes worked backwards to steps that reached the hint. The researchers call this motivated reasoning.

Other studies find odd gaps. In the "reversal curse" paper, GPT-4 answered questions like "Who is Tom Cruise's mother?" correctly 79% of the time, and the reverse, like "Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son?", only 33% of the time (Berglund et al., 2023). A person who knows one direction usually knows the other. A model that mostly saw a fact one way round may not.

So "it's just autocomplete" undersells what's happening, and "it thinks like us" oversells it. A more honest summary: there's real internal structure, it's uneven in ways that are hard to predict from outside, and the model's own story about its reasoning isn't reliable evidence.

What the model doesn't carry

When a teammate says a release feels risky, they aren't only predicting the next sentence. They remember the last incident, the support team that's already stretched and the customer who called twice this week. If it goes wrong, they're the ones who answer for it.

An LLM has none of that unless you put it in the prompt. It doesn't know about the customer who called twice. It won't get paged at 2 a.m. It can talk about risk fluently, sometimes better than you would, but talking about consequences and owning them are different jobs. What AI can't know from the prompt alone goes deeper on that gap.

Two mistakes, both expensive

Decide that LLMs understand nothing and you leave real value on the table. A model can surface an assumption you missed, list edge cases, translate jargon or walk a beginner through a hard idea without anyone feeling silly for asking.

Decide that they understand the way a person does and you start treating fluent output as checked judgment. You accept citations without opening them. You let the model rank priorities that belong to the team. You ask it to settle a disagreement before anyone has written down the real constraints. The danger is an answer that sounds reasonable enough for you to stop thinking too early.

Match your checks to the stakes

A more useful question than "does it understand?" is "what kind of understanding does this task need, and who supplies which part?"

TaskWhat the model bringsWhat you still add
Brainstorming names or anglesBreadth and speedTaste: picking the one that fits
Explaining unfamiliar codeFast reading of patterns it has seen many timesA run or a test that confirms the behavior
Summarizing a long threadCompression and structureA check that nothing important fell out
Legal, medical, financial or security callsA draft and a list of questions to askPrimary sources, an expert and a named owner
A production design decisionOptions and trade-offsThe real constraints, failure modes and the final call

Habits that keep you in charge

  • Give it the real context: constraints, audience, what already failed. The model can't use what it never saw.
  • Ask it to name its assumptions and to say what would change its answer.
  • Don't treat its explanation of its own reasoning as proof. Check the output itself: run the code, open the source, redo the math.
  • When a fact matters, ask in both directions. The reversal curse is cheap to test.
  • Keep drafting and deciding separate. "Useful, not yet owned" is a fine status for any AI answer.

Try this week

  • Next time an AI answer feels convincing, mark which parts are pattern, which have evidence and which need your judgment.
  • Ask a model how it reached an answer, then confirm the answer some other way.
  • Pick one task you hand to AI often and fill in its row of the table above.

The speed is real, and enjoying it is fine. Just keep one question handy after the first impression: which part of this answer is pattern, which part is evidence, and which part still needs a person?

faqs.a: Experts disagree: a 2022 survey of NLP researchers split almost exactly in half on the question. Interpretability research shows real internal structure, such as chaining two facts to answer a question, alongside odd gaps, such as knowing a fact in one direction but not the reverse. Treat it as a different kind of understanding with its own blind spots.

faqs.q: Why do LLMs sound as if they understand?
faqs.a: They're trained to predict text across huge amounts of writing, which teaches them grammar, common facts and the usual shape of answers. When that pattern fits your question, the reply reads as thoughtful, even when the model has no access to your context and nothing riding on the outcome.

faqs.q: Can I trust an LLM's explanation of its own reasoning?
faqs.a: Not as proof. Anthropic's 2025 interpretability work found Claude 3.5 Haiku solved a sum one way internally and then described a different, textbook method when asked. Check the output itself by running the code, reading the source or redoing the calculation.

faqs.q: How should teams use LLMs safely?
faqs.a: Match the check to the stakes. Use LLMs freely for drafts, summaries and options. For legal, medical, financial, security or production decisions, verify against primary sources, involve someone with domain knowledge and keep a named person responsible for the final call.
